what.text: Hexarelin is a lab-made peptide of six amino acids. It is a growth hormone-releasing peptide (GHRP), related to GHRP-6. WADA lists it by its official name, examorelin.

src.label: Laron et al., Clin Endocrinol (Oxf), 1995
WADA 2026 Prohibited List

what.text: In people it causes strong growth hormone release after injection into a vein or under the skin, by nose spray or by mouth. It also raises other hormones: cortisol, ACTH and prolactin.

src.label: Rahim et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 1998
Frieboes et al., Psychoneuroendocrinology, 2004

what.text: Heart studies suggest it also acts directly on receptors for growth hormone secretagogues in heart muscle, apart from its effect on growth hormone.

src.label: Broglio et al., Eur J Pharmacol, 2002
Bisi et al., Eur J Pharmacol, 1999

what.text: Hexarelin is not an approved medicine. Using it for sleep or anything else is off-label and outside any approval.

research.text: Human studies of hexarelin are small and mostly from the 1990s and early 2000s. Most gave a single dose and measured hormones or heart pumping. The one sleep study found it reduced deep sleep. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no hexarelin trial.

research.title: Hexarelin and sleep in healthy volunteers, 2004

facts.v: placebo-controlled; four injections of hexarelin (4 x 50 micrograms) or placebo between 10 pm and 1 am, with sleep EEG recorded
7 young healthy volunteers
one night per condition
sleep stages and EEG delta power; night-time GH, ACTH, cortisol, prolactin, leptin and immune markers

research.found: Deep sleep (stage 4) in the first half of the night and delta power over the whole night fell significantly with hexarelin. GH and prolactin rose all night; ACTH and cortisol rose in the first half. The authors concluded sleep was impaired after hexarelin.

src.label: Frieboes et al., Psychoneuroendocrinology, 2004

research.title: Twice-daily injections for 16 weeks, 1998

facts.v: open study, no placebo group
adults (number not given in the abstract)
16 weeks of injections under the skin, then 4 weeks off
GH response to a test dose; IGF-1; bone markers; body composition; bone density

research.found: The GH response shrank by week 4 and stayed lower at week 16, then recovered 4 weeks after stopping. IGF-1, body fat, lean mass and bone density did not change significantly.

src.label: Rahim et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 1998

research.title: Nasal spray in short children, 1995

facts.v: open study, no placebo group
8 short children aged 4 to 11, before puberty
up to 8 months
IGF-1 and growth rate

research.found: IGF-1 rose and growth rate rose from 5.3 to 8.3 cm per year. The authors saw no apparent undesirable side effects.

src.label: Laron et al., Clin Endocrinol (Oxf), 1995

research.title: One dose in healthy men, 1999

facts.v: single intravenous dose of hexarelin or growth hormone, on separate occasions
7 healthy male volunteers
90 minutes after each dose
heart pumping (ejection fraction) by radionuclide scan; hormones

research.found: Hexarelin raised ejection fraction from 64% to 71%, lasting up to 60 minutes. Growth hormone at a matched level did not. Hexarelin, but not growth hormone, raised cortisol.

src.label: Bisi et al., J Endocrinol Invest, 1999

research.title: One dose in heart patients, 1999 to 2002

facts.v: single intravenous doses, compared with controls, GHRH, growth hormone or placebo
7 men with growth hormone deficiency; 13 people with severe heart failure from cardiomyopathy; 24 men during heart bypass surgery
minutes to hours after one dose
ejection fraction and other heart measures

research.found: Ejection fraction rose in men with GH deficiency and in ischemic cardiomyopathy, but not in dilated cardiomyopathy. In bypass surgery, hexarelin raised ejection fraction and cardiac output for up to 90 minutes; GHRH, growth hormone and placebo did not. None of these studies tested long-term use or outcomes.

src.label: Bisi et al., Eur J Pharmacol, 1999
Imazio et al., Eur J Heart Fail, 2002
Broglio et al., Eur J Pharmacol, 2002

research.text: In rats with an induced heart attack, two weeks of hexarelin injections raised stroke volume and cardiac output and lowered vascular resistance, similar to growth hormone. This is animal evidence only.

research.text: No registered trial of hexarelin was found as of November 1, 2026.

us.text: Hexarelin is not FDA approved for any use, and no company holds an approval for it. It is not on FDA’s lists of bulk substances nominated for compounding. Products sold online labelled “for research use only” or “not for human consumption” are not legal to sell for people to use. As of November 1, 2026.

after.text: Hexarelin is prohibited at all times under WADA class S2.2.4, growth hormone releasing factors, which names “GH-releasing peptides (GHRPs) [e.g. alexamorelin, examorelin (hexarelin), GHRP-1, … GHRP-6].” All S2 substances are non-Specified. It is still named on the 2027 list.

side.text: There is no drug label for hexarelin. Safety data come from small, short studies, and research-labelled products have no quality standard.

items.text: in the 2004 study, deep sleep fell after hexarelin.

src.label: Frieboes et al., Psychoneuroendocrinology, 2004

items.text: hexarelin raises cortisol, ACTH and prolactin, not only growth hormone. A 16-week study looked at this because repeated spikes of these hormones were a concern; the cortisol response was lower after 16 weeks.

unconfirmed: The number of people in the 1998 16-week study (Rahim et al.) is not given in the abstract, and the full paper was not opened.
Status in the UK, the EU and Australia was not checked against a regulator record (TGA’s ARTG search did not load; EMA search was blocked).
We found no FDA statement naming hexarelin specifically; the research-use statements cited are FDA’s general warnings about research-labelled drugs.
surprises: The only sleep study of hexarelin (7 volunteers, 2004) found that it reduced deep sleep, while a 1997 study of the oral secretagogue ibutamoren reported more deep sleep; GH secretagogues do not all act alike on sleep.
